newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels thrust north and west, witnesses.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels thrust north and west, witnesses.

text.p: Zairean rebels pushed north and west towards towns held by the Zairean army on Thursday and Ugandan troops patrolled the streets of at least one Zairean town which they seized last week.

Travellers arriving in the eastern Zairean town of Kasindi from the frontlines to the north said rebels were advancing towards the towns of Watsa and Isiro and the northeastern regional capital of Kisangani, Zaire's fourth largest city.
"Wherever they reach, the local population celebrates and many Zairean soldiers join their ranks," said one man from the town of Beni, which the rebels said they had seized last week.
"In the Beni and Bunia areas, civilians were celebrating the fall of the towns," he added. The rebels said they seized Bunia on Saturday and Ugandan military sources said it fell on Monday.
Residents of another town east of Kasindi however said they heard Bunia was still occupied by rampaging Zairean troops.

Ugandan troops, backed by artillery, clearly held Kasindi despite Ugandan military spokesmen saying Ugandan troops only pushed three km (two miles) into Zaire last week in hot pursuit of Moslem Ugandan rebels.
A commander in the Ugandan army, the Ugandan People's Defence Forces (UPDF), told Reuters: "UPDF troops will pull out of the Zairean towns of Kasindi and Virunga in two days' time."
"We have crushed the (Ugandan) rebels and it is time to go home. But the Zairean government must give us assurances that rebels will not continue attacking us from Zairean territory."
Kisindi is 10 km (six miles) west of the Ugandan border.

In Butembo, a member of the rebel-held town's crisis committee, a collection of local civil authorities, described the fighting style of the Zairean rebel gunmen, known as the Alliance of Democratic Force for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.
"What the alliance do is make the Mai-Mai go in front of them, then (the alliance fighters) come behind them fighting.
"What always happens is that when the Mai-Mai are about 15 km (nine miles) away, the Zaireans, the enemy, flee," he said.
The Mai-Mai are a militia force allied with the Tutsi Banyamulenge who rebelled in October when the Zairean government ordered all Banyamulenge to leave or be hunted down as rebels.

A truckload of Mai-Mai fighters drove through Butembo on Thursday, draped in garlands of grass, sprinkling water which they say protects them from bullets and loosing off volleys of automatic fire in the air.
The truck also carried the coffins of some of their dead.
Butembo is held by the Mai-Mai. Their fighters, wearing an odd assortment of uniforms and T-shirts, including one on a seven-year fighter saying "I'm in a Zoo", patrol the streets.
Zairean volunteers from the International Committee of the Red Cross said a total of 98 dead, rebels and civilians, had been buried in recent days including 58 in the town of Beni.
Butembo is 45 km (28 miles) south of Beni and 200 km (125 miles) north of the rebel-held North Kivu capital of Goma.
Aid sources said a plane headed on Thursday to Kisangani, which appeared quiet despite rebels saying it was surrounded.
In Kinshasa, Zairean officials said they were worried the country's demoralised soldiers were helping the Rwandan-backed rebel offensive by alienating local people before rebels arrive.

"It is the same now as it was in Goma and Bukavu more than a month ago," a government official said. "The rebels announce they are coming days in advance. The soldiers loot the town and disappear hardly putting up resistance."
The chief editor of the local Catholic church radio station in Kisangani told Reuters there was no sign of rebels within 50 km (35 miles) of the city, but the army itself was a problem.

The United States on Wednesday delivered a message to rebel leader Laurent Kabila, urging him to end murders and other human rights abuses against refugees returning to Rwanda and saying it would never support the creation of an artifical state in Zaire.
But the rebels already control a strip of Zairean territory 550 km (340 mile) long, running north-south parallel to the Rwanda and Uganda borders. They say their aim is Kinshasa.

The rebels have succeeded in blocking the deployment through their territory of a multinational force to help hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and Zaireans, arguing its real aim would be to restore President Mobutu Sese Seko's grip on power.
